meta.titre: Word Formation: building nouns, adjectives and adverbs from base words
meta.sous_theme: Prefixes, suffixes and changes of word class

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L English Language past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In a Yaoundé market, a customer praises a seller by saying, "You are honest, and your honesty is why I buy from you." Later she adds that he always weighs the goods honestly. The same root appears as an adjective, a noun and an adverb, and each form fits only one position in a sentence. GCE English papers test this skill in gap-fill items and in directed questions such as changing nouns to adverbs. If you can see how a word family is built, you can handle both.

items: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea, an adjective describes a noun, and an adverb usually describes a verb.
A prefix is added to the beginning of a word and a suffix to the end.
An abstract noun names a quality or idea, such as honesty or freedom.

sections.titre: How English words are built and changed
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Building a family of words

Most English words belong to a family built on a base word, also called a root. A **suffix** added at the end changes the word class (noun, verb, adjective or adverb). A **prefix** added at the beginning changes the meaning. A word formation question asks you to write or choose the form that the sentence needs.

### Common endings by word class

| Class | Common endings | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | -ness, -ity, -ment, -tion, -ance, -ence, -ship, -hood, -dom, -ism, -y | kindness, generosity, development, information, importance, patience, friendship, childhood, freedom, tourism, honesty |
| Adjective | -ful, -less, -able, -ible, -ous, -ive, -al, -ic, -ish, -ent, -ant | careful, careless, reliable, possible, dangerous, active, national, economic, foolish, patient, important |
| Verb | -ise or -ize, -en, -ify | modernise, widen, simplify |
| Adverb | -ly | quickly, happily |

### Negative prefixes

The prefixes un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-, non- and mis- give an opposite or a wrong sense. The right choice depends on the base word. Im- is used before b, m and p (impossible, immature, impatient). Il- is used before l (illegal) and ir- before r (irregular). Un- is the most common with adjectives (unhappy, unfair). Dis- appears with many verbs, adjectives and nouns (disagree, dishonest, disorder).

### Spelling changes

- A final y after a consonant becomes i before an ending: happy, happily, happiness.
- Adjectives ending in -le change to -ly in the adverb: possible, possibly; simple, simply.
- Adjectives ending in -ic usually take -ally: economic, economically.
- An adjective ending in -ful keeps both l's and adds -ly: careful, carefully.
- A few adverbs drop the final e: true, truly.

### Reading the gap

First decide the word class the gap needs. After *a*, *the* or *their* the gap is usually a noun or an adjective. After *be* or *seem* it is usually an adjective. If it describes a verb it is an adverb. Then decide the meaning: a clause such as *so he complained* or *but it failed* tells you whether the word is positive or negative. Finally check the spelling.

variantes.nom: Chains between nouns, adjectives and adverbs
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must change abstract nouns into adverbs, or adverbs into nouns
variantes.contenu_markdown: Go through the adjective. Noun to adverb: first find the adjective, then add *-ly*. Courage, courageous, courageously. Danger, dangerous, dangerously. Patience, patient, patiently. Happiness, happy, happily. Adverb to noun: remove *-ly* to find the adjective, then find the noun that names the same idea. Honestly, honest, honesty. Bravely, brave, bravery. Wisely, wise, wisdom. Freely, free, freedom. Successfully, successful, success. Pick out the words exactly as they appear in the text, change only the form, and give the number of answers the question asks for.

variantes.nom: Gap with a base word given
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the base word appears in capitals or brackets beside the gap
variantes.contenu_markdown: The base word is the starting point, not the answer. Decide the class the gap needs, then add or change the ending. If the base word is already the right class, the change is probably a prefix. In *The traveller was ______ (PATIENT)*, the base word is already an adjective, so the answer is formed with a negative prefix, not a suffix.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When four forms of the same word are offered
variantes.contenu_markdown: Cross out options of the wrong class first. If several options have the right class, choose by meaning (positive or negative) and then by spelling. Read the whole sentence again with your choice in place.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Complete the sentence with the correct form of the word in capitals.

*The traveller was ______ with the long delay at the motor park, so he complained loudly.* (PATIENT)

etapes.action: Decide the word class the gap needs.
etapes.justification: The gap comes after *was* and before *with*, so it needs an adjective that describes the traveller.

etapes.action: Compare the class with the base word.
etapes.justification: PATIENT is already an adjective, so no suffix is needed. The change must be a prefix.

etapes.action: Use the clause that follows to find the meaning.
etapes.justification: He *complained loudly*, so he did not stay calm. The word must be negative.

etapes.action: Choose the prefix from the first letter of the base word.
etapes.justification: PATIENT begins with p, and im- is used before p.

etapes.action: Write the word and read the sentence again.
etapes.justification: The new word keeps the spelling of the base word and fits the grammar and the meaning.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The answer is **impatient**: *The traveller was impatient with the long delay at the motor park, so he complained loudly.* The route was: word class, then prefix or suffix, then meaning, then spelling.

items.pourquoi_faux: Un- is the commonest negative prefix, but this word takes im-, which is used before p. The word *unpatient* does not exist in standard English.
items.correction_markdown: Write **impatient**. Check the first letter of the base word: im- before b, m and p.

items.pourquoi_faux: A final y after a consonant changes to i before an ending, so happy must become happily.
items.correction_markdown: Write **happily**. The same rule gives happiness.

items.pourquoi_faux: True is one of the few adjectives that lose the final e before -ly.

items.erreur_markdown: Filling the gap in *They admired their ______ (GENEROUS)* with **generous**.
items.pourquoi_faux: The gap follows *their*, so it needs a noun. An adjective cannot stand there.
The adverb is the whole adjective *beautiful* plus -ly. The l of -ful and the l of -ly both stay, so the ending is -fully, not -fuly.

items.enonce_markdown:
Write the adverb formed from each adjective.

(a) sad  (b) comfortable  (c) economic  (d) true
items.solution_markdown:
(a) sad becomes **sadly**: just add -ly.

(b) comfortable ends in -le, so the -le becomes -ly: **comfortably**.

(c) economic ends in -ic, so it takes -ally: **economically**.

(d) true drops the final e: **truly**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Read the sentence below. Pick out two abstract nouns and change each of them into an adverb.

*Her honesty and her bravery impressed the judges.*
items.solution_markdown:
The abstract nouns are honesty and bravery. Go through the adjective: honesty, honest, honestly; bravery, brave, bravely.

The adverbs are **honestly** and **bravely**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Complete each sentence with the correct form of the word in capitals.

(a) It is ______ to finish the road before the rains, so the contractors need more workers. (POSSIBLE)

(b) The mayor spoke ______ about the new market. (PASSION)

(c) The villagers' ______ to help made the work easier. (WILLING)
items.solution_markdown:
(a) After *is* we need an adjective, and the clause after the comma shows the meaning is negative. Im- is used before p: **impossible**.

(b) The word describes the verb *spoke*, so it is an adverb. passion, passionate, passionately: **passionately**.

(c) After *the villagers'* we need a noun. willing, willingness: **willingness**.

items_markdown: Decide the word class of the gap first: noun, adjective, verb or adverb.
Suffixes change the class of a word and prefixes change its meaning.
Im- is used before b, m and p, il- before l, and ir- before r.
To change a noun into an adverb, go through the adjective and add -ly; to change an adverb into a noun, go back to the adjective first.
Check spelling changes: happily, possibly, economically, truly.
